## What changed

What the first real machine this was pointed at turned up.

**`proxy test` needed root, though it is documented as the one command that
does not.** The temporary apt proxy config was always written under
`/var/lib/gitlab-upgrade`, which only root can write — so the diagnostic failed
with `EACCES` before its first probe. That is precisely backwards: you run the
diagnostic *before* you have sudo. When the state directory is not writable the
file now goes to a private temporary directory instead, created with `mkdtemp`
rather than a predictable name, and still `0600` — the proxy password is
protected exactly as before.

**The OS ceiling stopped the upgrade path early — by a full major version on
Ubuntu 20.04.** `data/os-matrix.json` claimed focal tops out at 17.7 and bionic
at 15.2; the repository actually publishes 18.11.11 for focal and 16.11.10 for
bionic. On top of that, a ceiling is written as a minor series (`16.11` means
all of 16.11.x), but the comparison treated the missing patch as zero and cut
the last series off entirely. Both are fixed, and the numbers are now checked
against `apt-cache madison` with the official repository attached, with the
date and source recorded in the file.

**The background-migration check never worked, on any version of GitLab.** It
called `m.failed`, and `scope :failed` does not exist in `BatchedMigration` —
not in any release from 14.10 to 19.1. The model defines the *state*
`failed`, and GitLab itself writes `with_status(:failed)`. So the query raised
`NoMethodError` every time: `doctor` always reported the migration state as
undeterminable, a warning `--force` clears, which means the critical finding
for *failed* migrations — the one documented as not clearable by `--force` —
could never fire. Worse, `run` waits for migrations between steps with the same
query, and would have polled a broken query for its full 72-hour timeout
instead of either waiting for migrations or stopping on failed ones. The
fixture that should have caught this was keyed on a copy of the same broken
string, so it answered the wrong question and stayed green; both the check and
the wait now read one shared constant, and the fixture is keyed on it.

**The SOCKS tunnel connected to the proxy itself, not to the target.** In the
`socksConnect` call, a `...proxy` spread sat after `host` and `port` and
overwrote them with the proxy's own address. So `proxy test` reported
`✓ CONNECT packages.gitlab.com:443` while actually connecting to
`proxy:1080` — and the TLS rung that followed was handshaking with a SOCKS
port, which of course drops it. The diagnostic pointed confidently at a host
nothing had contacted. The same call sat in `openSocket`, so notifications
through a SOCKS proxy went nowhere either; there is now one function instead of
two copies of the same defect. The TLS verdict is no longer one-size-fits-all:
a handshake cut mid-flight is not a certificate refusal, and there are now
separate rungs for "closed mid-handshake" and "this address is filtered" — the
latter established by probing a control host through the same proxy, because
"the proxy is broken" and "this address is blocked" send you to different
people.

**Background migrations are now counted on every version, including 13.x.**
`BatchedMigration` only appeared in 13.11; below that the constant does not
exist, so the check could not work at all on the versions this tool exists to
climb out of. Older migrations live in the Sidekiq queue
(`Gitlab::BackgroundMigration.remaining`, present from 13.0 to 17.11) and were
not counted at all, though leaving 13.x without draining them is exactly what
you must not do. A missing constant is now skipped; a missing *method* is not —
`NoMethodError` inherits from `NameError`, and a blanket rescue would have
turned the broken call above into a silent "no migrations". The reply names
which mechanisms answered, so "we asked the wrong question" can no longer read
as "nothing pending".

**The installer now copes with several Node installations on one machine.**
`sudo` sees a different `PATH` than you do, and a server carrying an old
`/usr/local/bin/node` next to a current one in `nvm` would be refused outright.
The installer looks past `PATH`, pins the interpreter it found, and takes
`--node` if you would rather choose. When root ends up pinned to an interpreter
owned by someone else — a `nvm` build in a user's home — it says so plainly:
anyone who can rewrite that file gets root, and a system-wide Node is the way
out. `--probe-host` and `--probe-timeout` were read by `proxy test` but never
actually declared as options; they exist now.
